### Utilities for R.

# Necessary packages
packages_required <- c(
  "knitr", "tidyverse", "vegan", "permute",
  "ggrepel", "grid", "dplyr", "readxl", "glmmTMB",
  "DHARMa", "car", "emmeans", "ggnewscale"
)
# Already installed?
packages_installed <- vapply(
  packages_required, 
  FUN = requireNamespace, 
  FUN.VALUE = TRUE, 
  quietly = TRUE
) 
# Install missing packages
install.packages(names(packages_installed)[!packages_installed])

# Chunk font size hook: allows size='small' 
# or any valid Latex font size in chunk options
def.chunk.hook <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("chunk")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(
  chunk = function(x, options) {
    x <- def.chunk.hook(x, options)
    ifelse(
      options$size == "normalsize", 
      yes = x,
      no = paste0("\n \\", options$size, "\n\n", x, "\n\n \\normalsize")
    )
  }
)

#load all packages
invisible(lapply(packages_required, library, character.only = TRUE))

# Set output width to prevent long model summaries overflowing PDF margins
knitr::opts_chunk$set(width = 65)

#set seed for reproducible simulations throughout the document
set.seed(123)

Code acknowledgement for the code above: The initial Quarto setup and package-management code were adapted from Eric Marcon’s TP-Biodiversity-2026 repository. The code was subsequently modified and extended for the following analysis.

df <- read_excel("../data/macrofauna_counts.xlsx")
df[7:ncol(df)] <- lapply(df[7:ncol(df)], as.numeric)
df[c(1, 3:6)] <- lapply(df[c(1, 3:6)], as.factor)

1.2 Setting figure color scheme (colorblind-checked)

# readability verified deuteranopia, protanopia, tritanopia and on greyscale

layer_colors <- c(
  "L"  = "#AFC8B5",
  "10" = "#B47A2C",
  "20" = "#355C7D"
)

soil_colors <- c(
  "alt" = "#C5A36A",
  "dls" = "#394B45"
)

taxon_colors <- c(
  "Formicidae" = "#B56B32",
  "Isoptera" = "#496987",
  "Lumbricina_oligochaetes" = "#527F68",
  "Others" = "#A6A39B"
)

2 Statistical Analysis

2.1 Data preparation for GLMM:

# identify taxa columns
taxa_cols <- names(df)[7:34]

# long-format dataset
df_long <- df %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(taxa_cols),
    names_to = "taxon",
    values_to = "count"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    taxon = factor(taxon)
  )

# sample-level abundance (per m²)
df_total <- df %>%
  mutate(
    total_count = rowSums(
      across(all_of(taxa_cols)),
      na.rm = FALSE
    ),
    density = total_count * 16, #25x25cm monoliths = 1/16 m²
    soil_type = factor(soil_type),
    layer = factor(layer, levels = c("L", "10", "20")),
    monolith_ID = factor(monolith_ID)
  )

2.2 Explorative Analysis

2.2.1 Key values

# Boxplot of total macrofauna density
fig_density <- ggplot(
  df_total,
  aes(
    x = layer,
    y = density,
    fill = soil_type
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.7,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    outlier.shape = 1
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = soil_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(
  trans = scales::pseudo_log_trans(base = 10),
  breaks = c(0, 10, 100, 1000, 5000),
  labels = scales::label_comma()
) +
  labs(
    x = "Soil layer",
    y = expression("Total density (ind. m"^{-2}*")"),
    fill = "Soil type"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

print(fig_density)

The difference of total density between ALT and DSL seems not evident on the graph. The layer 10 seems have higher density that 20 and L bit not difference between 20 and L.

# Convert taxonomic data to long format
df_long <- df %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = 7:34,
    names_to = "taxon",
    values_to = "count"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    taxon = factor(taxon)
  )

# Group taxa into the three focal groups and others
composition <- df_long %>%
  mutate(
    taxon_group = case_when(
      taxon == "Formicidae" ~ "Formicidae",
      taxon == "Isoptera" ~ "Isoptera",
      taxon == "Lumbricina_oligochaetes" ~ "Lumbricina_oligochaetes",
      TRUE ~ "Others"
    ),
    layer = factor(layer, levels = c("L", "10", "20")),
    taxon_group = factor(
      taxon_group,
      levels = names(taxon_colors)
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(soil_type, layer, taxon_group) %>%
  summarise(
    total = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  group_by(soil_type, layer) %>%
  mutate(
    proportion = total / sum(total)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Plot taxonomic composition
fig_composition <- ggplot(
  composition,
  aes(
    x = soil_type,
    y = proportion,
    fill = taxon_group
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    colour = "white",
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ layer) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent,
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = taxon_colors,
    drop = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Soil type",
    y = "Proportion of individuals",
    fill = "Taxon"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

print(fig_composition)

Formicidae, Isoptera and Lumbricina are the most abundant groups in our samples. The other groups have been gathered together because their respective small abundance. The abundances of the tree mains group seems changed between layers : Formicidae are more abundant in the 20 layer but seems dominated in each soil types and layers. Isoptera are nearly absent in the layer 20, but they dominate as Formicidae in the layer 10 and layer L in ALT. Lumbricina are absent in the layer L, and seem more abundant in the layer 20 than 10.

2.2.2 PCA

# Community matrix
comm <- as.matrix(df[, taxa_cols])
storage.mode(comm) <- "numeric"

# Remove samples with zero total abundance
keep <- rowSums(comm) > 0 # one removed

comm_pca <- comm[keep, , drop = FALSE]

# Hellinger transformation
comm_hel <- vegan::decostand(comm_pca, method = "hellinger")

# PCA
pca <- prcomp(
  comm_hel,
  center = TRUE,
  scale. = FALSE
)

# Percentage of variance explained
variance_pca <- 100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)

# Scores and metadata
scores_pca <- as.data.frame(pca$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  mutate(
    soil_type = df$soil_type[keep],
    layer = factor(df$layer[keep], levels = c("L", "10", "20")),
    monolith_ID = df$monolith_ID[keep]
  )

# Taxon coordinates from PCA loadings
taxa_scores <- as.data.frame(pca$rotation[, 1:2]) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("taxon") %>%
  mutate(
    cos2 = PC1^2 + PC2^2
  )

# Scale taxon arrows to fit sample scores
arrow_scale <- min(
  diff(range(scores_pca$PC1)) / diff(range(taxa_scores$PC1)),
  diff(range(scores_pca$PC2)) / diff(range(taxa_scores$PC2))
) * 0.7

taxa_scores <- taxa_scores %>%
  mutate(
    PC1_arrow = PC1 * arrow_scale,
    PC2_arrow = PC2 * arrow_scale
  )

# Keep taxa reasonably represented on the first two PCA axes
taxa_scores_plot <- taxa_scores %>%
  filter(cos2 >= 0.10) # can change cos2 here

1 sample has to be removed for PCA due to zero abundance

fig_pca <- ggplot(
  scores_pca,
  aes(
    x = PC1,
    y = PC2,
    colour = soil_type,
    shape = layer
  )
) +

  # Reference lines at the origin
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dotted",
    colour = "grey65",
    linewidth = 0.4,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dotted",
    colour = "grey65",
    linewidth = 0.4,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +

  # Confidence ellipses by soil type
 stat_ellipse(
  data = scores_pca,
  mapping = aes(
    x = PC1,
    y = PC2,
    group = soil_type,
    colour = soil_type
  ),
  level = 0.95,
  type = "t",
  linetype = "dashed",
  linewidth = 0.7,
  show.legend = FALSE,
  inherit.aes = FALSE
) + 

  # Sample scores
  geom_point(
    size = 3,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +

  # Discrete colour scale for soil type
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = soil_colors,
    name = "Soil type"
  ) +

  # Start a separate colour scale for taxon arrows
  ggnewscale::new_scale_colour() +

  # Taxon arrows, coloured by cos2
  geom_segment(
    data = taxa_scores_plot,
    aes(
      x = 0,
      y = 0,
      xend = PC1_arrow,
      yend = PC2_arrow,
      colour = cos2
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    arrow = grid::arrow(
      length = grid::unit(0.2, "cm")
    ),
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +

  # Taxon labels, coloured by cos2
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = taxa_scores_plot,
    aes(
      x = PC1_arrow,
      y = PC2_arrow,
      label = taxon,
      colour = cos2
    ),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 3.5,
    max.overlaps = Inf,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +

  # Continuous colour scale for taxon cos2
  scale_colour_gradient(
    low = "grey80",
    high = "#2166AC",
    name = expression(cos^2)
  ) +

  # Layer shapes
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(
      "L" = 16,
      "10" = 17,
      "20" = 15
    ),
    name = "Layer"
  ) +

  # Axis labels
  labs(
    x = paste0(
      "PC1 (",
      round(variance_pca[1], 1),
      "%)"
    ),
    y = paste0(
      "PC2 (",
      round(variance_pca[2], 1),
      "%)"
    )
  ) +

  # Theme
  theme_bw()

fig_pca

2.3 GLMM with abundances

2.3.1 GLMM global

2.3.1.1 Fitting the models:

Models to investigate effects of soil_type and layer on abundance. Poisson and negative binomial models are considered since abundances are counts and there may be a tendency to overdispersion or zero-inflation.

# M1: Poisson, additive effects
m_p_add <- glmmTMB(
  total_count ~ soil_type + layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = df_total
)

# M2: Poisson, interaction
m_p_int <- glmmTMB(
  total_count ~ soil_type * layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = df_total
)

# M3: Negative binomial, additive effects
m_nb_add <- glmmTMB(
  total_count ~ soil_type + layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"),
  data = df_total
)

# M4: Negative binomial, interaction
m_nb_int <- glmmTMB(
  total_count ~ soil_type * layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"),
  data = df_total
)

2.3.1.2 Comparing models using Akaike’s An Information Criterion

AIC_values <- AIC(m_p_add, m_p_int, m_nb_add, m_nb_int)

AIC_values$delta_AIC <- AIC_values$AIC - min(AIC_values$AIC)

AIC_values[order(AIC_values$AIC), ]
         df      AIC  delta_AIC
m_nb_add  6 490.2159   0.000000
m_nb_int  8 494.0688   3.852888
m_p_int   7 660.1740 169.958110
m_p_add   5 665.2099 174.993989

Negative binomial distribution is strongly preferred according to AIC and is retained.

2.3.1.3 Comparing nb additive vs. model with interaction:

anova(m_nb_add, m_nb_int) #likelihood ratio test LRT
Data: df_total
Models:
m_nb_add: total_count ~ soil_type + layer + (1 | monolith_ID), zi=~0, disp=~1
m_nb_int: total_count ~ soil_type * layer + (1 | monolith_ID), zi=~0, disp=~1
         Df    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Chi Df Pr(>Chisq)
m_nb_add  6 490.22 502.78 -239.11   478.22                         
m_nb_int  8 494.07 510.82 -239.03   478.07 0.1471      2     0.9291

Given the interactive model has a higher AIC and does not significantly improve model fit compared to additive model (according to LRT), m_nb_add is retained.

2.3.1.4 Model diagnostics with DHARMa:

res_nb <- simulateResiduals(m_nb_add, n = 1000)
plot(res_nb)
testDispersion(res_nb)

    DHARMa nonparametric dispersion test via sd of residuals fitted vs.
    simulated

data:  simulationOutput
dispersion = 1.4118, p-value = 0.374
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
testZeroInflation(res_nb)

    DHARMa zero-inflation test via comparison to expected zeros with
    simulation under H0 = fitted model

data:  simulationOutput
ratioObsSim = 0.75188, p-value = 1
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

No significant deviations detected, model is retained.

Type II Wald chi-square tests revealed a highly significant effect of soil layer on total soil macrofauna abundance (\(\chi^2\) = 106.85, df = 2, p < 0.001). The effect of soil type was not significant (\(\chi^2\) = 0.52, df = 1, p = 0.469). Estimated random-effect variance (monolith) was 0.437 (SD = 0.661), indicating variation in baseline macrofauna abundance among monoliths.

2.3.1.6 Pairwise testing for layers:

# Estimated marginal means for layers (response scale)
emm_layers <- emmeans(m_nb_add, ~ layer, type = "response")

# Pairwise comparisons (Tukey correction)
pairwise_layers <- as.data.frame(
  pairs(emmeans(m_nb_add, ~ layer), adjust = "tukey")
)

# Back-transform estimates to abundance ratios
pairwise_layers$ratio <- exp(pairwise_layers$estimate)
pairwise_layers
 contrast   estimate        SE  df z.ratio p.value    ratio
 L - 10   -2.0043646 0.2198861 Inf  -9.115 <0.0001 0.134746
 L - 20   -0.1827018 0.2334295 Inf  -0.783  0.7137 0.833017
 10 - 20   1.8216628 0.2184400 Inf   8.339 <0.0001 6.182129

Results are averaged over the levels of: soil_type 
Results are given on the log (not the response) scale. 
P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 3 estimates 
# Plot estimated abundance on the response scale
plot(emm_layers)

Pairwise comparisons with Tukey adjustment shows that macrofauna abundance was significantly higher in layer 10 than in layers L (7.42 times) and 20 (6.18 times), while no significant difference was found between layers L and 20 (p = 0.714).

2.3.2 GLMM ecosystem engineers

2.3.2.1 Formicidae (Ants)

df_ants <- df_total %>%
  select(Formicidae, layer, monolith_ID, soil_type)

# M1: Poisson, additive effects
ants_p_add <- glmmTMB(
  Formicidae ~ soil_type + layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = df_ants
)

# M2: Poisson, interaction
ants_p_int <- glmmTMB(
  Formicidae ~ soil_type * layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = df_ants
)

# M3: Negative binomial, additive effects
ants_nb_add <- glmmTMB(
  Formicidae ~ soil_type + layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"),
  data = df_ants
)

# M4: Negative binomial, interaction
ants_nb_int <- glmmTMB(
  Formicidae~ soil_type * layer + (1 | monolith_ID),
  family = nbinom2(link = "log"),
  data = df_ants
)

AIC_ants <- AIC(ants_p_add, ants_p_int, ants_nb_add,ants_nb_int)

AIC_ants$delta_AIC <- AIC_ants$AIC - min(AIC_ants$AIC)

AIC_ants[order(AIC_ants$AIC), ]
            df      AIC delta_AIC
ants_nb_add  6 403.2416    0.0000
ants_nb_int  8 407.0212    3.7796
ants_p_int   7 544.2341  140.9925
ants_p_add   5 564.8352  161.5936

We keep the negative binomial distribution for the engineers because the AIC is lower that Poisson distribution models.

Quantile deviation detected (upper quantile specifically). Some relatively high-abundance observations may not be adequately captured by the model. Since all the other tests do not show any significant issues, ants_nb_add is retained as best-supported model regardless, though unexplained structure might remain.

Type II Wald chi-square tests revealed a significant effect of soil layer on earthworm abundance (\(\chi^2\) = 12.69, df = 2, p = 0.0018). The effect of soil type was not significant (\(\chi^2\) = 0.35, df = 1, p = 0.557). The estimated random-effect variance for monolith was 0.510 (SD = 0.714), indicating variation in baseline earthworm abundance among monoliths. The model summary shows that estimates including layer were highly instable, with standard errors of around 10511. Coefficients can therefore not be correctly interpreted for layers.

Pairwise comparisons with Tukey adjustment showed significantly higher abundance in layer 10 than in layer 20 (2.31 times). No significant differences were detected between layer L and either layer 10 or layer 20 (both p = 1.000). However, the estimated abundance of earthworms in layer L was zero with an unbounded confidence interval. No earthworms were observed in layer L during the sampling, which explains the high errors in the models and the unbounded confidence interval.

2.4 PERMANOVA

2.4.1 Data preparation

df_perm <- df
# defining taxonomic abundance columns
community_cols <- names(df_perm)[7:ncol(df_perm)]

# remove zero-abundance samples (decision following vegan
#handbook, since zero-abundance layer does not convey community
#composition information)
keep <- rowSums(df_perm[, community_cols], na.rm = TRUE) > 0
df_perm <- df_perm[keep, , drop = FALSE]

# create the community matrix
comm <- as.matrix(df_perm[, community_cols])
storage.mode(comm) <- "numeric" # making sure its num

# define meta_layer for tested variables + monoliths
meta_layer <- df_perm[, c("monolith_ID", "soil_type", "layer")] 

# create Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrix
dist_layer <- vegdist(comm, method = "bray")

2.4.2 PERMANOVA layer effects

# Bray-Curtis PERMANOVA
# define permutation scheme, limit WITHIN monoliths (due to
#spatial dependence of the three layers)
perm_layer <- how(
  nperm = 9999,
  blocks = meta_layer$monolith_ID
) # chose large number of perms for stabilizing p value, increase
#for borderline p values

# run based on defined scheme
permanova_layer <- adonis2(
  dist_layer ~ layer,
  data = meta_layer,
  permutations = perm_layer
)

print(permanova_layer)

# => significant, R2 16%

PERMANOVA shows a significant effect of soil layer on macrofauna community composition (Bray–Curtis dissimilarity: F = 5.46, R² = 0.163, p = 0.0001). Soil layer explained around 16.3% of variation in the community composition, indicating that macrofauna community composition differed significantly among layers.

# check dispersion using betadisper (if significant, permanova
#result might only be due to unequal dispersion; a bit like
#homogeneity of variance in anova) / is like non-parametric
#Levene test

bd_layer <- betadisper(
  dist_layer,
  group = meta_layer$layer,
  type = "median",
  bias.adjust = TRUE
)

# same permutation scheme

dispersion_layer <- permutest(
  bd_layer,
  permutations = perm_layer
)

print(dispersion_layer)

Homogeneity of multivariate dispersion was assessed using a permutation test based on betadisper. No significant differences in dispersion were detected for soil layers (F = 0.75, p = 0.321), suggesting that the PERMANOVA result was not driven by differences in within-group dispersion.

# pairwise PERMANOVA testing for layers
layer_pairs <- list(
  c("L", "10"),
  c("L", "20"),
  c("10", "20")
)

# function based to apply to all pairs
pairwise_results <- lapply(layer_pairs, function(pair) {
  
  # Keep only the two layers being compared
  keep_pair <- meta_layer$layer %in% pair
  
  meta_pair <- droplevels(meta_layer[keep_pair, , drop = FALSE])
  
  # subset the original Bray-Curtis distance object for this pair
  dist_pair <- as.dist(as.matrix(dist_layer)[keep_pair, keep_pair])
  
  # restrict perms to monoliths, like in global PERMANOVA
  perm_pair <- how(
    nperm = 9999,
    blocks = meta_pair$monolith_ID
  )
  
  # perform PERMANOVA
  res <- adonis2(
    dist_pair ~ layer,
    data = meta_pair,
    permutations = perm_pair
  )
  
  #for nice table notation
  data.frame(
    comparison = paste(pair, collapse = " vs "),
    F = res$F[1],
    R2 = res$R2[1],
    p_value = res$`Pr(>F)`[1]
  )
})

pairwise_results <- do.call(rbind, pairwise_results)

# Correct for the three pairwise tests
pairwise_results$p_adjusted <- p.adjust(
  pairwise_results$p_value,
  method = "bonferroni" ) # Bonferroni correction

print(pairwise_results)
  comparison        F        R2 p_value p_adjusted
1    L vs 10 6.053937 0.1406129   2e-04      6e-04
2    L vs 20 4.553169 0.1095745   1e-04      3e-04
3   10 vs 20 5.755480 0.1315374   3e-04      9e-04

Pairwise PERMANOVA suggests significant differences in macrofauna community composition for all soil layers. Significant differences were observed between L and 10 (F = 6.05, R² = 0.141, adjusted p = 0.0003), L and 20 (F = 4.55, R² = 0.110, adjusted p = 0.0003), and 10 and 20 (F = 5.76, R² = 0.132, adjusted p = 0.0012), using Bonferroni correction.

2.4.3 PCoA for layers

# calculate, using same distance matrix like in PERMANOVA
pcoa_layer <- cmdscale(
  dist_layer, k = 2, eig = TRUE, add = TRUE
) # set k for number of dimensions +> k = 2 two dimensional

# sample scores
pcoa_df_perm <- data.frame(
  PCoA1 = pcoa_layer$points[, 1],
  PCoA2 = pcoa_layer$points[, 2],
  layer = factor(df_perm$layer, levels = c("L", "10", "20"))
)

# calculate hulls around samples
hull_df_perm <- pcoa_df_perm %>%
  group_by(layer) %>%
  slice(chull(PCoA1, PCoA2))

# fit taxon abundances to the PCoA (using same permutation scheme
#as in PERMANOVA)
fit <- envfit(
  pcoa_layer$points,
  comm,
  permutations = perm_layer
)

# extract taxon results and adjust p-values (multiple testing)
taxa_results <- data.frame(
  taxon = rownames(fit$vectors$arrows),
  R2 = fit$vectors$r,
  p_value = fit$vectors$pvals
)

taxa_results$p_adjusted <- p.adjust(
  taxa_results$p_value,
  method = "BH"
) # BH adjustment for multiple testing (false discovery rate)

# extract taxon vectors 
vec <- as.data.frame(scores(fit, display = "vectors"))
vec$taxon <- rownames(vec)
names(vec)[1:2] <- c("PCoA1", "PCoA2")

# match adjusted p-values by taxon
vec$p_adjusted <- taxa_results$p_adjusted[
  match(vec$taxon, taxa_results$taxon)
]

# keep those with adjusted p < 0.05
vec <- vec[
  !is.na(vec$p_adjusted) &
    vec$p_adjusted < 0.05,
]

# calculate dim1 and dim2 percentages
eig <- pcoa_layer$eig
positive_eig <- eig[eig > 0]

pc1_pct <- 100 * eig[1] / sum(positive_eig)
pc2_pct <- 100 * eig[2] / sum(positive_eig)


# plot PCoA
p <- ggplot(pcoa_df_perm, aes(PCoA1, PCoA2, color = layer)) +
  geom_polygon(
    data = hull_df_perm,
    aes(x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2, fill = layer, group = layer),
    alpha = 0.12,
    color = NA,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = layer_colors) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = layer_colors) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "PCoA of macrofauna communities by layer",
    color = "Layer",
    fill = "Layer",
    x = sprintf("PCoA1 (%.1f%%)", pc1_pct),
    y = sprintf("PCoA2 (%.1f%%)", pc2_pct)
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "right"
  )


# taxon arrows and labels
  p <- p +
    geom_segment(
      data = vec,
      aes(
        x = 0, y = 0,
        xend = PCoA1, yend = PCoA2
      ),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      color = "grey25",
      linewidth = 0.9,
      arrow = arrow(
        length = unit(0.2, "cm"),
        type = "closed"
      )
    ) +
    geom_label_repel(
      data = vec,
      aes(
        x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2,
        label = taxon
      ),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      color = "grey15",
      fill = alpha("white", 0.6),
      label.size = NA,
      size = 3.5,
      fontface = "italic",
      box.padding = 0.6,
      point.padding = 0.5,
      force = 3,
      max.overlaps = Inf,
      min.segment.length = Inf,
      segment.color = NA,
      seed = 123
    )

print(p)

  filter(p_adjusted < 0.05) %>%

The first two PCoA axes accounted for 26.1% of the variation in macrofauna community composition (PCoA1: 15.8%; PCoA2: 10.3%). The ordination showed partial separation of communities among soil layers. Samples from layers L and 20 exhibited substantial overlap, whereas samples from layer 10 were more distinctly shifted towards the right of the ordination.

The envfit analysis identified four taxa significantly associated with the ordination: Isoptera (R² = 0.501, adjusted p = 0.0014), Chilopoda (R² = 0.183, adjusted p = 0.0014), Opiliones (R² = 0.155, adjusted p = 0.0103) and Lumbricina_oligochaetes (R² = 0.238, adjusted p = 0.0154). Isoptera showed the strongest association with the ordination.

2.4.4 PERMANOVA for soil types

# sum across all layers within each monolith => to test
#independent of layer effects, since dependent of monolith
comm_mono <- rowsum(
  comm,
  group = df_perm$monolith_ID,
  reorder = FALSE
)

# one metadata row per monolith
meta_mono <- df_perm[
  !duplicated(df_perm$monolith_ID),
  c("monolith_ID", "soil_type")
]

# aligning matrix with metadata
comm_mono <- comm_mono[
  as.character(meta_mono$monolith_ID),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

Is aggregated per monolith since layers are not independent. Only tests between soils on monolith level.

dist_soil <- vegdist(comm_mono, method = "bray")
# Bray-Curtis PERMANOVA

permanova_soil <- adonis2(
  dist_soil ~ soil_type,
  data = meta_mono,
  permutations = 9999
) 

print(permanova_soil)

Residual 18   3.8162 0.91473

# not significant, no differences by soil type

# betadisper

bd_soil <- betadisper(
  dist_soil,
  group = meta_mono$soil_type,
  type = "median",
  bias.adjust = TRUE
)

dispersion_soil <- permutest(
  bd_soil,
  permutations = 9999
)

print(dispersion_soil)

PERMANOVA did not show a significant difference in macrofaunal community composition between soil types (F = 1.68, R² = 0.085, p = 0.139). The test for homogeneity of multivariate dispersion was also non-significant (F = 0.11, p = 0.742), indicating no detectable difference in within-group dispersion between soil types.
